slides.title: Introduction
slides.content: Introduction Vocabulary: {sky, wings, engine, helicopter, drone, rocket, goose, eagle, bee} How do we determine what constitutes this vocabulary? The goose is in the sky. The eagle in the sky has wings. The bee in the sky has wings. The goose with wings in the sky. The eagle with wings in the sky. The bee with wings in the sky. The goose and the eagle with wings are in the sky. The goose flies in the sky. The wings of the bee are good wings. The helicopter, the drone and the rocket are in the sky. The helicopter in the sky is a useful engine. The drone in the sky is an engine that takes pictures. A rocket is an engine. The helicopter is an engine. A drone is an engine that takes pictures. A rocket is a useful engine among sky engines. A helicopter is flying in the sky. The sky is full of helicopters and drones. The engine here is a drone, the one there is a rocket. Toy corpus 2 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Regular expressions
slides.content: Regular expressions Regular expressions: disjunctions Pattern Matches [wW]oodchuck Woodchuck, woodchuck [1234567890] Any one digit Letters inside brackets Pattern Matches Examples [0-9] A single digit Chapter 1: Down the Hole [A-Z] An upper case letter Drenched Blossoms [a-z] A lower case letter my beans were impatient Ranges using the dash 9 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Regular expressions
slides.content: Regular expressions Regular expressions: Negation in disjunction Pattern Matches Examples [^A-Z] Not an upper case letter Drenched Blossoms [^Ss] Neither S nor s my beans were impatient [^.] Not a period Our resident Djinn [e^] Either e or ^ Look up ^ now Carat as ﬁrst character in [] negates the list Note • Special characters (., ∗, +, ?) lose their special meaning inside [] • Carat means negation only when it’s ﬁrst in [] 10 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Regular expressions
slides.content: Regular expressions Regular expressions Pattern Expansion Matches Examples \d [0-9] Any digit Latitude 59 \D [^0-9] Any non-digit Blue moon \w [a-zA-Z0-9_] Any alphanumeric or _ Daiyu \W [^\w] Not alphanumeric or _ Look! \s [\r\t\n\f] Whitespace Look␣up \S [^\s] Not whitespace Look up Convenient aliases 11 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Regular expressions
slides.content: Regular expressions Regular expressions Groundhog is another name for woodchuck! Pattern Matches groundhog|woodchuck woodchuck yours|mine yours a|b|c Abba [gG]roundhog|[wW]oodchuck Woodchuck Using the pipe symbol | for disjunction 12 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Regular expressions
slides.content: Regular expressions Regular expressions False positives and false negatives This process is based on ﬁxing two kinds of errors: • Not matching things that we should have matched (The) False negatives • Matching strings that we should not have matched (there, then, other) False positives 17 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Regular expressions
slides.content: Regular expressions Regular expressions False positives and false negatives The process involves two antagonistic eﬀorts in reducing the error rate: • Increasing coverage (or recall) (minimizing false negatives). • Increasing accuracy (or precision) (minimizing false positives) This is characteristic of much work in NLP Note: If you do not know about the recall, precision and F1 metrics, check the extra videos and slides. 18 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Regular expressions
slides.content: Regular expressions Regular expressions Use case: put angles around all numbers e.g. the 35 boxes →the <35> boxes Group capturing • Parentheses () capture a pattern into a numbered register (1,2,3) • Use \1 to refer to the contents of the register: s/([0-9]+)/<\1>/ 21 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Regular expressions
slides.content: Regular expressions Regular expressions Group capturing: multiple registers /the (.*)er they (.*), the \1er we \2/ • Matches the faster they ran, the faster we ran • But not the faster they ran, the faster we ate 22 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Regular expressions
slides.content: Regular expressions Regular expressions Non-capturing groups Add ? : after the opening parenthesis: /(?:some|a few) (people|cats) like some \1/ • some cats like some cats matches • some cats like some some does not match 23 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Regular expressions
slides.content: Regular expressions Regular expressions Use case: match the letter q but only if it is not followed by the letter u (match q in faqir but not in question) Lookahead assertions • (?! pattern) (negative lookahead): is true if pattern does not match , but is zero-width: it doesn’t advance the character pointer /q(?!u)/ • (?= pattern) (positive lookahead): is true if pattern matches, but is zero-width Note: the textbook is short and unclear on this topic, this link is better, or this video. We’ll also see examples in the lab. 24 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Word tokenzation and normalization and sentence segmentation
slides.content: Word tokenzation and normalization and sentence segmentation Word tokenization Tokenization in NLTK Bird and Loper (2004) »> import nltk »> text = 'That U.S.A. poster-print costs $12.40...' »> pattern = r'''(?x) # set flag to allow verbose regexps (?:[A-Z]\.)+ # abbreviations | \w+(?:-\w+)* # words with optional internal hyphens | \$?\d+(?:\.\d+)?%? # currency and percentages | \.\.\. # ellipsis | [][.,;"'?():_`-] # these are separate tokens ''' »> nltk.regexp_tokenize(text, pattern) ['That', 'U.S.A.', 'poster-print', 'costs', '$12.40', '...'] 32 NLP: Tokenization

slides.content: Word tokenzation and normalization and sentence segmentation Word normalization Case folding • Reducing all letters to lower case may be useful in some applications, e.g. IR where users tend to use lower case • Possible exception: upper case in mid-sentence • Apple vs apple • March vs march • Turkey vs turkey • Case is helpful in other applications, e.g. MT or IE • US vs us 37 NLP: Tokenization

slides.content: Word tokenzation and normalization and sentence segmentation Sentence segmentation Split by punctuation !, ? mostly unambiguous but period“.”is very ambiguous • Sentence boundary • Abbreviations like Inc. or Dr. • Numbers like .02% or 4.3 Two-step procedure 1. Classify periods as part of the word or sentence boundary • Using rules Using a regex or an abbreviation dictionary • Using ML 2. Based on this, segment sentences by rules. 40 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Subword tokenization
slides.content: Subword tokenization Subword tokenization Subwords Determined in a data-driven way, using a compression algorithm. Common ones: • Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE; Sennrich et al. (2016)) • Unigram language model (Kudo, 2018) • WordPiece (Schuster and Nakajima, 2012) Subword tokenizers components • Token learner: induces a vocabulary from a training corpus. • segmenter: tokenizes a raw (test) sentence according to that vocabulary. 43 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Subword tokenization
slides.content: Subword tokenization Outline Introduction Regular expressions Basics Applications Word tokenzation and normalization and sentence segmentation Word tokenization Word normalization Sentence segmentation Subword tokenization BPE Subword tokenization: limitations Summary 44 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Subword tokenization
slides.content: Subword tokenization Subword tokenization BPE algorithm Let the vocabulary be the set of all individual characters {A, B, C, D,…, a, b, c, d….} Repeat: Choose the two symbols that are most frequently adjacent in the training corpus (say A, B) Add a new merged symbol AB to the vocabulary Replace every adjacent A B in the corpus with AB. Until k merges have been done. 45 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Subword tokenization
slides.content: Subword tokenization Subword tokenization BPE: notes • Most subword algorithms are run inside space-separated tokens ⇒before training: • Add a special end-of-word symbol (e.g. ’_’) before spaces in the training corpus • Separate into letters. • For eﬃciency, bigrams that cross word boundaries are not considered 46 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Subword tokenization
slides.content: Subword tokenization BPE token segmenter On the test data, run each merge learned from the training data: • Greedily • In the order we learned them ⇒merge every e r to er, then merge er _ to er_, etc. Result • n e w e r _ would be tokenized as a full word • l o w e r _ would be two tokens: low er_ 50 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Subword tokenization
slides.content: Subword tokenization Subword tokenization: limitations Example tokenization result by GPT-4o. • Subwords are determined based on frequency, they are not (necessarily) linguistically meaningful. 52 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Subword tokenization
slides.content: Subword tokenization Subword tokenization: limitations Example tokenization result by GPT-4o. • Subwords are determined based on frequency, they are not (necessarily) linguistically meaningful. • Subwords are suboptimal for morphologically complex languages (Klein and Tsarfaty, 2020) • The vocabulary of multilingual LLMs is dominated by English. • This leads to longer sequences for non-English languages, which is more costly and less accurate (Ahia et al., 2023). 53 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Subword tokenization
slides.content: Subword tokenization Subword tokenization: addressing the limitations • Subwords are determined based on frequency, they are not (necessarily) linguistically meaningful. Subword tokenizers can be modiﬁed to be informed by morphology (see lecture 7) • Subwords are suboptimal for morphologically complex languages (Klein and Tsarfaty, 2020) Alternative units of representation? (next slide) • The vocabulary of multilingual LLMs is dominated by English. • This leads to longer sequences for non-English languages, which is more costly and less accurate (Ahia et al., 2023). Allocate vocabulary more fairly across languages (e.g. Foroutan et al. (2025)) 54 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Subword tokenization
slides.content: Subword tokenization Subword tokenization: addressing the limitations Alternatives to subwords • Character-based models (Lee et al., 2017) • Byte-based models (Wang et al., 2020) • Pixel-based models (Rust et al., 2023) Limitations Characters and bytes lead to long sequences. Pixel-based representations lag behind subwords in terms of accuracy. (But we are working on bridging this gap!) 55 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Subword tokenization
slides.content: Subword tokenization Subword tokenization and alternatives • A long ignored but increasingly active area of research • Recently got its own workshop TokShop • Nice invited talks with videos online (if you are curious): Yuval Pinter overview of the evolution of tokenization Desmond Elliott Pixel-based models 56 NLP: Tokenization

slides.title: Summary
slides.content: Summary Summary Regular expressions • are a useful tool for language processing, • were previously the main technique for tokenization, • are still used nowadays for pre-processing (or pre-tokenization) and normalization, prior to subword tokenization, • are still used for sentence segmentation. Subwords • are learned in a data-driven way, with a compression algorithm, • have limitations. • Overcoming these limitations is an open challenge. 58 NLP: Tokenization
